Annual Crop Land: Annual Crop Land has rectangular or polygonal field parcels with sharp, straight boundaries that reflect human-imposed geometric regularity.
Annual Crop Land shows a mosaic pattern of adjacent plots with contrasting tones or textures due to varying crop types or growth stages.
Annual Crop Land contains fine-textured vegetation or bare soil within each parcel, lacking the dense, continuous dark canopy of Forest.
Annual Crop Land features access tracks and farm roads aligned precisely with field edges, forming a grid-like network.
Annual Crop Land displays uniform texture inside individual parcels but strong textural variation between neighboring parcels.
Annual Crop Land lacks the repeated dot or grid pattern of tree crowns seen in Permanent Crop Land.
Annual Crop Land exhibits more sharply bounded and regularly shaped cultivated parcels than the irregular, diffuse grassy expanses of Pasture Land.
Annual Crop Land commonly includes visible drainage or irrigation lines running parallel to field boundaries.
Annual Crop Land shows patches of bare soil or mixed soil-vegetation tones, unlike the consistently green, closed-canopy cover of Herbaceous Vegetation Land.
Annual Crop Land has field parcels sized typically between 0.5 and 5 hectares, smaller and more numerous than large-scale pasture blocks.
Annual Crop Land contains linear features such as straight-field-edge ditches that are absent in naturally formed wetland or forest edge patterns.
Annual Crop Land lacks the clustered, irregular building arrangements typical of Rural Settlement Land.
Annual Crop Land shows no standing water bodies larger than narrow irrigation channels or temporary field ponds.
Annual Crop Land has minimal or no tree cover within parcels, distinguishing it from Agroforestry Land where trees are interspersed with crops.
Annual Crop Land displays high spatial organization in vegetation distribution, contrasting with the patchy, unmanaged growth of Shrubland.
Annual Crop Land features field boundaries defined by low-contrast soil lines or subtle elevation changes rather than hedgerows or tree rows.
Annual Crop Land contains no visible orchard-style tree spacing or vineyard trellis patterns found in Permanent Crop Land.
Annual Crop Land shows seasonal variation in dominant color—brown or tan during fallow/plowing, green during growth—but always with parcel-level uniformity.
Annual Crop Land lacks the sinuous, natural meandering of rivers or streams cutting across fields, as those features would indicate non-agricultural land use.
Annual Crop Land has no built-up area density exceeding isolated farm structures, distinguishing it clearly from Urban or Industrial Land.
Forest: Forest is characterized by large, contiguous patches of vegetation with irregular, soft boundaries that follow natural terrain contours rather than straight-line parcel edges.
Forest exhibits dominant dark green to deep green tones across the canopy, significantly darker than the medium green of herbaceous vegetation land.
Forest shows a coarse, mottled texture from overlapping tree crowns, unlike the smoother, more uniform texture of pasture land.
Forest lacks visible internal field divisions such as plow lines or harvest striping commonly seen in cropland.
Forest contains few or no paved roads, with any linear features appearing narrow, winding, and discontinuous rather than forming a grid.
Forest has minimal to no built structures, with roof density substantially lower than in urban or rural settlement classes.
Forest displays shadowed crown structure creating variable brightness within the canopy, contrasting with the even illumination of bare soil or water surfaces.
Forest features spatial patterns aligned with natural drainage networks and topographic ridges rather than orthogonal street grids.
Forest shows high vegetation density with near-continuous canopy cover, leaving little exposed ground visible compared to sparse woodland or shrubland.
Forest lacks regular row patterns or evenly spaced tree alignments typical of permanent crop land orchards or plantations.
Forest contains no visible geometric parcel boundaries defined by fences, ditches, or hedgerows as found in agricultural land.
Forest has low contrast between adjacent patches due to homogeneous vegetation cover, unlike the sharp tonal transitions between fields in cropland.
Forest exhibits branching, dendritic linear features (e.g., small streams) rather than straight, engineered canals or irrigation ditches.
Forest shows muted color variation across the scene, with limited presence of brown (bare soil), white (roofs), or blue (water) pixels.
Forest contains no visible rectangular or square building footprints arranged in clusters or along roadsides as in rural residential areas.
Forest has no evidence of regularly spaced utility poles, power lines, or linear infrastructure corridors cutting through the canopy.
Forest displays gradual tonal gradients across slopes rather than abrupt, flat-toned surfaces associated with paved parking lots or airport runways.
Forest lacks the fine-grained, repetitive texture of irrigated rice paddies or other flooded agricultural fields.
Forest shows no visible water bodies larger than narrow streams or small ponds, distinguishing it from wetland or aquatic classes.
Forest maintains consistent visual complexity at multiple spatial scales—coarse texture remains evident even when zoomed out—unlike the simplified, blocky appearance of built-up land.
Herbaceous Vegetation Land: Herbaceous Vegetation Land shows broad, irregularly shaped patches of land cover with naturalistic, non-rectilinear boundaries.
Herbaceous Vegetation Land displays a continuous, soft-textured surface without the coarse, shadowed canopy texture of Forest.
Herbaceous Vegetation Land lacks the straight, parallel plow lines and geometric row structure characteristic of Annual Crop Land.
Herbaceous Vegetation Land has no evenly spaced planting points or repeated linear striping seen in Permanent Crop Land.
Herbaceous Vegetation Land exhibits minimal built structure density, with few or no buildings compared to urban or suburban land classes.
Herbaceous Vegetation Land features green to yellow-brown dominant tones that shift seasonally but remain distinct from the deep greens of dense forest canopies.
Herbaceous Vegetation Land shows no paved roads, highways, or rectilinear street grids typical of urban or transport infrastructure.
Herbaceous Vegetation Land contains no open water bodies, smooth water surfaces, or linear river corridors with defined banks.
Herbaceous Vegetation Land lacks the enclosed paddock subdivisions, fence lines, or managed pasture boundaries common in Pasture Land.
Herbaceous Vegetation Land presents a fine-grained, fairly uniform grassy texture rather than the patchy, mixed-height vegetation of shrubland or woodland edge.
Herbaceous Vegetation Land occupies large areal extents without the narrow linear corridors of transportation or irrigation infrastructure.
Herbaceous Vegetation Land shows no rooftop patterns, building footprints, or clustered residential or industrial structures.
Herbaceous Vegetation Land has no visible cultivated field blocks segmented by sharp, angular parcel boundaries.
Herbaceous Vegetation Land displays surface irregularity and organic shape variation unlike the engineered symmetry of orchard or vineyard layouts.
Herbaceous Vegetation Land contains no dark, high-contrast tree crowns or dense woody canopy clusters that dominate Forest.
Herbaceous Vegetation Land lacks the bright, reflective surfaces of rooftops, solar panels, or paved parking lots.
Herbaceous Vegetation Land shows no evidence of irrigation ditches, canals, or regularly spaced agricultural infrastructure.
Herbaceous Vegetation Land features low vegetation density with few scattered trees, contrasting with the closed-canopy continuity of Forest.
Herbaceous Vegetation Land has no visible livestock enclosures, barns, or farmstead clusters associated with managed Pasture Land.
Herbaceous Vegetation Land exhibits diffuse, unstructured patch edges rather than the sharp, human-defined borders of cultivated or developed land.
Highway or Road: Highway or Road is a narrow, elongated corridor with uniform width extending continuously across the scene, unlike rivers which meander and vary in width.
Highway or Road appears as a straight or gently curved linear feature with sharp, well-defined edges, contrasting with the irregular, organic boundaries of rivers or forest edges.
Highway or Road exhibits strong geometric regularity with parallel edges maintained over long distances, unlike building clusters which form irregular angular patches.
Highway or Road displays a smooth, homogeneous surface texture with minimal internal variation, whereas building clusters show heterogeneous textures from roofs, walls, and shadows.
Highway or Road is predominantly gray, white, or dark gray in color, lacking the green tones of adjacent vegetation or the reddish-brown hues of bare soil.
Highway or Road occupies a thin linear footprint rather than a compact, area-filling patch like a building complex or industrial yard.
Highway or Road shows high contrast between its constructed surface and immediately adjacent vegetation or bare ground, more pronounced than the gradual transitions seen at field boundaries.
Highway or Road forms continuous linear connectivity linking intersections and junctions, unlike isolated roads or trails that terminate abruptly within undeveloped land.
Highway or Road maintains consistent alignment and orientation across large portions of the scene, unlike agricultural field boundaries which follow irregular topographic contours.
Highway or Road lacks internal segmentation or texture variation along its length, distinguishing it from rail lines which often show periodic ties or ballast patterns.
Highway or Road is bordered by relatively narrow roadside strips or shoulders, not by wide vegetated buffers or riparian zones typical of rivers.
Highway or Road appears as a single dominant linear element within an otherwise non-linear urban fabric, unlike grid-like street networks where multiple intersecting lines create blocky patterns.
Highway or Road has angular intersections with other roads at consistent right or acute angles, unlike natural drainage channels that fork asymmetrically.
Highway or Road shows no visible water surface, reflection, or sinuous flow pattern, clearly separating it from rivers and canals.
Highway or Road is spatially organized in planned corridors rather than clustered arrangements, unlike building groups which occupy contiguous, irregularly shaped parcels.
Highway or Road lacks the fine-scale texture and shadow variation associated with rooftop arrays or parking lots, appearing uniformly flat and unbroken.
Highway or Road is typically flanked by aligned development such as rows of buildings or trees, but the road itself remains a distinct, unbroken linear strip rather than merging into a built-up zone.
Highway or Road exhibits no branching into dendritic patterns like river tributaries, maintaining a primary trunk structure with limited, orthogonal offshoots.
Highway or Road has sharply defined, machine-straight margins without the soft, diffuse edges seen in dirt tracks or unpaved farm lanes.
Highway or Road displays no evidence of surface water pooling, sediment deposition, or vegetated banks, distinguishing it from seasonal streams or drainage ditches.
Industrial Buildings: Industrial Buildings have large rectangular roof footprints that dominate the scene, often arranged in clusters of identical warehouse or factory halls.
Industrial Buildings occupy broad paved yards and loading areas that extend far beyond building perimeters, creating extensive contiguous impervious surfaces.
Industrial Buildings feature buildings spaced farther apart on larger parcels than Residential Buildings, resulting in lower building density and more open paved space between structures.
Industrial Buildings show sharp, regular edges and block-like building geometries with high angular precision and minimal curvature.
Industrial Buildings display dominant gray, white, or dark-toned impervious cover with little variation in surface reflectance across large roof and yard areas.
Industrial Buildings exhibit organized layouts aligned to orthogonal road networks, with buildings oriented consistently along cardinal directions.
Industrial Buildings lack the repetitive parallel line patterns of Annual Crop Land, showing no field rows, furrows, or crop texture bands.
Industrial Buildings contain sparse, fragmented vegetation patches that are small, irregularly shaped, and isolated from one another, unlike the continuous green canopy of Forest or Woodland.
Industrial Buildings have wide access roads adjacent to building clusters, but these roads serve as connectors rather than dominant linear corridors like Transportation Corridors.
Industrial Buildings show no orchard grid patterns or regularly spaced tree canopies characteristic of Permanent Crop Land.
Industrial Buildings feature rectilinear building footprints with aspect ratios typically exceeding 2:1, distinguishing them from the more square or irregular shapes of Commercial Buildings.
Industrial Buildings include large open storage surfaces with uniform texture and no visible vegetation, unlike the mottled soil or stubble textures of recently harvested Cropland.
Industrial Buildings display minimal rooftop vegetation or green infrastructure, contrasting sharply with the frequent green roofs or vegetated surfaces seen in some Modern Residential complexes.
Industrial Buildings have low vegetation density overall, with less than 5% canopy cover in most parcels, far below the >30% typical of Grassland or Pasture.
Industrial Buildings show building clusters connected by straight, wide paved service roads rather than the narrow, winding, or dendritic street patterns of Residential Areas.
Industrial Buildings lack water bodies such as ponds, reservoirs, or rivers within their immediate parcel boundaries, unlike Aquaculture or Irrigated Cropland.
Industrial Buildings exhibit high geometric regularity in roof alignment, with over 90% of long building axes deviating less than 10 degrees from a common orientation.
Industrial Buildings contain loading docks and covered transfer zones visible as recessed rectangular indentations along building perimeters, absent in Office or Retail Building complexes.
Industrial Buildings feature large unbroken roof surfaces exceeding 5,000 m² each, substantially larger than the typical roof area of Small-Scale Residential or Institutional Buildings.
Industrial Buildings show paved surfaces with high albedo contrast between light-colored concrete and dark asphalt, forming distinct tonal boundaries not found in Natural Land Cover classes.
Pasture Land: Pasture Land is a large contiguous land parcel with irregular to moderately regular shapes that form open grazing enclosures rather than tightly cultivated plots.
Pasture Land shows dominant green to yellow-brown tones reflecting grassy vegetation cover at varying growth stages, without the stark seasonal bare-soil contrast seen in Annual Crop Land.
Pasture Land exhibits a fine, soft texture across the entire parcel surface, lacking the strong row patterns or plowed striping characteristic of Permanent Crop Land and Annual Crop Land.
Pasture Land displays clear, visible field boundaries—often linear or gently curved—that demarcate grazing enclosures, unlike the diffuse edges of Herbaceous Vegetation Land.
Pasture Land has sparse built structures, with few or no buildings scattered across the parcel, distinguishing it from Urban or Peri-Urban classes where building density is high.
Pasture Land features adjacent farm tracks or unpaved roads that follow parcel perimeters or bisect fields, rather than the dense grid of paved streets found in Urban classes.
Pasture Land lacks repeated linear planting geometry, making it visually distinct from Permanent Crop Land where orchards or vineyards show strict parallel rows.
Pasture Land contains no visible water bodies such as ponds, rivers, or irrigation canals within the parcel, unlike Aquaculture or Rice Paddy classes.
Pasture Land shows uniform vegetation density across the parcel, with no alternating bands of bare soil and crop cover typical of tilled Annual Crop Land.
Pasture Land has minimal or no tree cover across the parcel surface, contrasting sharply with Forest classes where canopy closure is near-complete.
Pasture Land occupies broad, open landscapes with low topographic relief visible in the terrain, unlike Mountain Pasture which shows pronounced slope gradients and rocky outcrops.
Pasture Land parcels often abut other agricultural fields but maintain distinct boundary lines, whereas Herbaceous Vegetation Land merges gradually into natural vegetation without sharp demarcation.
Pasture Land displays a patch-scale texture that is more homogeneous and intentional than the mottled, naturally patchy appearance of Herbaceous Vegetation Land.
Pasture Land rarely includes linear drainage ditches or geometric irrigation channels, differentiating it from intensively managed Rice Paddy or Vegetable Field classes.
Pasture Land shows no evidence of seasonal harvesting patterns like cut swaths or stubble fields, unlike Annual Crop Land which frequently exhibits recent mechanical disturbance.
Pasture Land parcels are typically larger in average size than those of Permanent Crop Land, which often consists of smaller, densely planted orchard or vineyard units.
Pasture Land lacks the high-contrast geometric repetition of greenhouse clusters or plastic-covered rows seen in Protected Horticulture classes.
Pasture Land has no visible silos, barns, or livestock infrastructure concentrated within the parcel, unlike Livestock Farming Infrastructure classes where such features dominate the scene.
Pasture Land exhibits gentle tonal transitions across the parcel surface, without the abrupt color shifts between crop types or fallow fields common in Mixed Cropland.
Pasture Land shows consistent low-height vegetation structure across the parcel, with no vertical heterogeneity or multi-layered canopy like that in Agroforestry or Forest Edge classes.
Permanent Crop Land: Permanent Crop Land has large contiguous parcels with sharp, straight-edged boundaries that contrast sharply with the irregular, jagged edges of natural vegetation.
Permanent Crop Land shows rectangular or elongated field shapes arranged in tightly packed, grid-like configurations unlike the more scattered and irregular parcel layouts of Pasture.
Permanent Crop Land displays regularly spaced linear rows of woody vegetation visible as parallel dark green stripes, distinct from the uniform green wash of Annual Crop Land.
Permanent Crop Land exhibits a repeating dot pattern at canopy level corresponding to individual trees or vines, unlike the continuous canopy texture of Forest.
Permanent Crop Land contains internal straight farm access tracks aligned precisely with crop rows, whereas Pasture lacks such geometrically aligned internal linear features.
Permanent Crop Land features terraced plots following contour lines with consistent step widths and sharp retaining edges, unlike the smooth, unstructured slopes of Natural Vegetation.
Permanent Crop Land shows alternating bands of darker green canopy and lighter-toned inter-row strips of bare soil or low grass, absent in the spectrally homogeneous cover of Herbaceous Land.
Permanent Crop Land has field boundaries oriented consistently across adjacent parcels—often north-south or east-west—unlike the variable, non-aligned boundaries of Annual Crop Land.
Permanent Crop Land reveals fine-scale grid-like texture at high resolution due to evenly spaced planting points, contrasting with the coarser, clumped texture of Shrubland.
Permanent Crop Land displays uniform canopy height and density within each parcel, producing consistent brightness and texture, unlike the vertically layered and variable reflectance of Mixed Forest.

Permanent Crop Land contains straight, narrow linear gaps between planted rows that persist across entire fields, whereas Vineyards classified as Permanent Crop Land show narrower, more frequent gaps than Orchard-type Permanent Crop Land.
Permanent Crop Land shows high spectral contrast between adjacent parcels due to uniform but differing crop types, unlike the low inter-parcel contrast in Pasture.
Permanent Crop Land exhibits elongated, parallel field shapes aligned along valley floors or gentle slopes, differing from the circular or amorphous shapes of Irrigated Pasture.
Permanent Crop Land has minimal internal texture variation within a single parcel, reflecting uniform plant age and spacing, unlike the patchy, age-mixed texture of Regenerating Forest.
Permanent Crop Land displays sharp transitions between vegetated rows and unvegetated inter-rows, creating high-frequency texture, unlike the low-frequency, smooth texture of Grassland.
Permanent Crop Land features field edges that follow precise right-angle corners and straight segments, unlike the curved, organic boundaries of Wetland.
Permanent Crop Land shows consistent row orientation maintained across multiple adjacent parcels, whereas Annual Crop Land often shifts orientation between fields due to seasonal tillage.
Permanent Crop Land contains sparse, evenly distributed tree canopies forming a perforated green surface, unlike the dense, closed-canopy green of Evergreen Forest.
Permanent Crop Land has parcels bounded by narrow, linear dirt or gravel tracks that form a hierarchical network, unlike the wide, paved roads that dissect Urban Land.
Permanent Crop Land presents a mosaic of similarly sized, geometrically regular parcels with minimal size variation, unlike the highly heterogeneous parcel sizes in Smallholder Agricultural Mosaic.
Residential Buildings: Residential Buildings are characterized by clusters of small to medium rectangular roof footprints arranged in tight proximity rather than isolated large building blocks.

Residential Buildings exhibit a dense network of narrow streets and driveways forming interconnected grids or cul-de-sac patterns, unlike the sparse or absent road networks in forested or agricultural land.

Residential Buildings show a high proportion of impervious surfaces including gray, white, or dark rooftops alongside paved driveways and sidewalks, contrasting with the continuous green canopy of deciduous forest.
Residential Buildings display parcelized, regularly spaced lots with sharp-edged boundaries and consistent setbacks, differing from the irregular, organic edges of wetlands or natural shorelines.

Residential Buildings feature a fine-grained spatial texture created by alternating roof patches, small yards, and scattered individual trees, unlike the uniform, large-scale monotony of industrial warehouse complexes.

Residential Buildings have buildings oriented along local street alignments with consistent frontage and setback distances, whereas industrial buildings often face loading docks perpendicular to access roads.
Residential Buildings contain minimal open paved areas beyond roads and driveways, distinguishing them from industrial zones dominated by expansive parking lots and service yards.

Residential Buildings show low-to-medium building density with visible gaps between structures filled by grass, shrubs, or small trees, unlike the near-continuous built coverage of high-density urban commercial districts.
Residential Buildings lack long, straight, parallel linear features typical of crop rows in annual cropland, instead showing short, branching, and curved residential streets.
Residential Buildings present a mosaic of varied roof colors—gray, beige, red, and black—rather than the monochromatic, uniformly reflective surfaces of solar farms or metal-roofed industrial sheds.

Residential Buildings include small, irregularly shaped vegetated patches interspersed among structures, contrasting with the large, contiguous, and uniformly textured tree canopies of mature coniferous forests.
Residential Buildings occupy patches that are typically 0.1–2 km² in extent, smaller and more fragmented than the vast, uninterrupted expanses of pastureland or rangeland.
Residential Buildings display right-angled intersections and orthogonal street layouts, unlike the meandering, dendritic patterns of rural country lanes or natural stream channels.
Residential Buildings feature buildings arranged in repeating block-like formations bounded by streets on all sides, differing from the linear, ribbon-style development along highways or rivers.
Residential Buildings contain no large water bodies or extensive shoreline features within the patch, distinguishing them from coastal residential clusters where water dominates the scene.
Residential Buildings show minimal or no large-scale geometric field boundaries such as those defining vineyards or orchards, relying instead on property lines and fence alignments.
Residential Buildings have low vertical relief variation across the patch, with roofs at similar elevations and no tall towers or silos common in industrial or energy infrastructure sites.
Residential Buildings exhibit scattered, low-canopy vegetation with variable density and species, unlike the dense, closed-canopy uniformity of plantation forests.
Residential Buildings lack the long, unbroken linear corridors of railroads or major highways that bisect or border industrial or transportation zones.
Residential Buildings contain no large, rectilinear, empty paved surfaces exceeding 50 m in width, distinguishing them from airport runways or intermodal freight terminals.
River: River is a long, narrow, elongated feature that traverses the scene rather than forming a broad enclosed basin.
River has a sinuous or branching channel pattern with visible bends and tributary-like connections.
River width varies gradually along its course instead of staying uniformly engineered.
River banks are irregular natural edges rather than straight paved margins or lane-marked surfaces.
River commonly borders thin strips of riparian vegetation that follow the channel closely.
River appears as a smooth or fine-textured surface compared with adjacent vegetated or built-up areas.
River exhibits darker blue, dark green, or gray tones depending on depth, sediment, and illumination.
River boundaries are often sharply contrasted against adjacent land cover.
River lacks internal roof patterns that distinguish built-up areas.
River lacks crop rows that characterize cultivated fields.
River lacks dense canopy texture seen in forested areas.
River forms a continuous connected shape rather than many small discrete objects.
River is visually distinct from lakes because it does not form a broad enclosed basin.
River is visually distinct from roads because its edges are irregular and unpaved, not straight and marked.
River is visually distinct from canals because its width changes gradually rather than remaining uniform.
River is visually distinct from reservoirs because it follows a natural sinuous path rather than an angular, geometric outline.
River is visually distinct from wetlands because it shows clear linear continuity and defined channel confinement rather than diffuse, patchy water saturation.
River is visually distinct from ponds because it extends across the scene as a single dominant linear feature rather than appearing as isolated small water bodies.
River is visually distinct from streams because it is wider and more consistently visible across larger spatial extents in satellite imagery.
River is visually distinct from drainage ditches because it displays natural branching tributaries and meanders rather than short, straight, grid-aligned segments.
Sea or Lake: Sea or Lake is a broad contiguous water expanse occupying a large area rather than a narrow elongated channel.
Sea or Lake has a compact, rounded, lobed, or irregular basin or coastal shape instead of a thin meandering linear form.
Sea or Lake exhibits a smooth or nearly textureless surface compared with vegetated or built-up areas.
Sea or Lake displays a generally uniform dark blue, blue-green, or gray tone across broad areas.
Sea or Lake lacks field boundaries, building footprints, or road grid patterns within the water surface.
Sea or Lake has edges defined by shorelines or banks that sharply separate water from land.
Sea or Lake contains specular brightness or sun-glint patches on parts of the surface.
Sea or Lake shows an interior that is largely uninterrupted by bars, banks, or frequent crossings that segment the feature.
Sea or Lake has a much greater width-to-length ratio than a river.
Sea or Lake occupies a wide open-water area enclosed or bordered by shoreline rather than flanked by parallel banks.
Sea or Lake shows no visible flow direction indicators such as sinuous current streaks or sediment plumes typical of rivers.
Sea or Lake lacks the dendritic or branching tributary network pattern characteristic of river systems.
Sea or Lake has no visible bridge crossings spanning its full width.
Sea or Lake displays no evidence of in-channel islands or midstream sandbars dividing the water body.
Sea or Lake shows no alignment with topographic contours indicating confined valley flow like a river.
Sea or Lake exhibits no gradual narrowing or widening along its length as seen in river reaches.
Sea or Lake has no visible dam structures or abrupt elevation changes interrupting continuity.
Sea or Lake shows no adjacent floodplain vegetation bands paralleling a central channel.
Sea or Lake contains no visible boat wakes or vessel traffic trails indicating directional movement.
Sea or Lake presents a static, unbroken water surface without the longitudinal streaking or turbidity gradients common in flowing rivers.
